Besides the political ramifications, the business ones are going to come home to roost. If every U.S. vendor is now a kill-switch risk, the allied market for that whole ecosystem shrinks. As it sinks into the European countries that the U.S, can simply shut off any technology, over time they will find and build alternatives. In the years ahead, this may cost American companies tens if not hundreds of billions of lost revenue.

The U.S. spent decades establishing itself as the world’s indispensable technology supplier. A substantial part of that advantage depended on customers believing American technology would remain reliable and available.

Going forward a U.S. founder selling into European defense or government now needs an answer to “who holds the switch” before the first meeting; and European founders just got sovereignty as a sellable feature.

items.title: AI-Assisted Paper on Z-Library Cites a TorrentFreak Article That Doesn't Exist
items.content:
Z-Library is one of the largest pirate ebook libraries on the Internet, offering millions of books and papers for free.

For students and researchers who can’t afford expensive textbooks and journal subscriptions, it can be a useful resource. At the same time, publishers have spent years trying to take it down, with takedown notices and blocking orders, while U.S. authorities indicted its alleged operators.

The peer-reviewed academic paper doesn’t pick a side and the lead author kindly shared a copy of their work with TorrentFreak. While the conclusions are not immediately newsworthy, there was one reference that stood out right away.

A TorrentFreak Article That Doesn’t Exist

In a section on enforcement against Z-Library, the authors write that major academic publishers, including Elsevier and Springer Nature, have taken similar legal action. The reference is a 2021 TorrentFreak article, as shown below.

The problem is that this particular legal action is new to us. The reference section lists the article as “Publishers continue crackdown on shadow libraries” and links to the TorrentFreak homepage. However, we have never published an article with that title.

Looking more closely, we see more claims that don’t seem to fit. The paper’s account of the Z-Library criminal case, for example, states that the U.S. Department of Justice “arrested individuals” in 2022.

The DOJ’s own press release says that the two alleged operators, whose indictment we covered at the time, were arrested in Argentina “at the request of the United States.” The title the paper gives for that press release doesn’t exist either.

These non-existent citations appear plausible, as they cite real publications and organizations in a fitting context. However, that doesn’t mean they are accurate. When we went over the full reference list, we noticed that this applies to more sources.

The paper cites a 2019 Harvard Journal of Law & Technology article by IP law professor Daniel Gervais, titled “The future of intellectual property in the shadow of shadow libraries.” The table of contents of the cited issue doesn’t include it, and the cited pages are taken up by two articles on other topics.

The same applies to a 2019 College & Research Libraries article attributed to Carol Tenopir and colleagues. The cited issue has no article by Tenopir. She did co-author a 2019 article on a similar topic, but it appeared in a different journal, under a different title.

Other references that couldn’t be located include a 2019 article credited to Björn Brembs and articles credited to authors named Smith, Piper, Okike and Aronson, as well as a Kaspersky report on “the hidden dangers of shadow libraries.”

In total, we had trouble finding at least ten of the 44 references in the paper, as well as others that didn’t necessarily back the stated claims.

The obvious question is where these mystery references came from. The paper’s acknowledgements may offer a hint in the right direction, as they mention that AI was used in the research and writing process.

“We confirm that Consensus AI was used in sifting through large volume of literature and extract relevant information,” the authors write. They add that ChatGPT was used to improve the language of parts of the paper.

AI chatbots are known to invent references, often with plausible titles credited to real experts in the field. This could explain the findings, although it doesn’t prove that AI wrote these references.

We also ran the paper’s abstract and conclusion through the AI detection tool Pangram. For both sections, the tool reported that “100% of the text is likely AI-generated.” These types of tools are not perfect and can produce false positives, but it would fit the picture.

It would be rather ironic if AI caused these errors. It would mean that a paper in a commercial, peer-reviewed journal, published by Taylor & Francis, relied on AI to write about Z-Library. Meanwhile, many rightsholders are suing AI companies for using shadow libraries to train AI models.

Interestingly, the paper explicitly warns that sites such as Z-Library hurt publishers’ revenue, which funds peer review and editing.

“The widespread use of Z-Library poses significant challenges to the sustainability of academic publishing. Publishers rely on subscription fees and paywalls to fund the peer review, editing, and distribution of scholarly works,” it reads, presumably generated by AI as well.

The paper doesn’t mention that peer reviewers generally aren’t paid for their work, an issue that was central to a recent lawsuit against major academic publishers, including Taylor & Francis.

The lead author initially shared a copy of the paper with us, but didn’t answer our follow-up questions about the mysterious references. We also asked Gervais, Brembs and Tenopir whether they wrote the papers that are credited to them, but they didn’t respond either.

Publisher Taylor & Francis did reply and says that it’s looking into the matter.

“I can confirm that this has been referred to our Editorial and Publishing Ethics & Integrity teams, who will investigate the concerns you have raised,” a Taylor & Francis spokesperson informed TorrentFreak.

The publisher will not comment further while the investigation is ongoing. Whether the paper will be corrected or retracted has yet to be seen.

The paper “Z-Library and Full-Text Access: Democratizing Knowledge or Undermining Copyright Ethics?” is available here.

Node2Shell evolves to HTTP2Shell, blast radius affects many HTTP libs and apps
items.content:
⚠️ Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 21st NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. On Thursday, Python disclosed that Python packages were vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 as well.

On Friday, October 23rd, it has become known that this CVE affects other major languages and service applications using HTTP, where patches are not yet fully available.

Check if you are decoding Brotli as a dependency within your libraries. Stay on guard for wider announcements and be ready to upgrade as soon as possible. If there is no patch available for a library or application that may be affected, we recommend disabling Brotli decoding until patches become available.

 Patches are available for libbrotli, Python, C++, NodeJS, bun, Envoy and more coming. Apache and Nginx do not decode brotli by default.

OpenAI shares that they discovered this vulnerability in February. While the root cause issue was fixed in the Brotli source code at the time, it wasn’t known that it gave rise to a security vulnerability. OpenAI's advisories here. ‍

Brotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It’s a way to make data smaller for storage or sending over the internet. Software then unpacks it to recover the original data. It’s widely used for HTTP compression to compress web content such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

CVE-2026-111497 is an out-of-bounds write in the Google Brotli decoder affecting versions 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 on all platforms. This is the same Brotli decoder flaw behind Node2Shell announced a couple days ago. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can send a crafted Brotli-compressed stream to corrupt memory, leak sensitive data, crash the process, or potentially execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), and Node.js is affected through its bundled Brotli library.

A bug makes the Brotli decoder keep accepting more bytes when it should reject the data. Those bytes can overflow a small working buffer and damage the program’s memory. An attacker can use that damage to control what runs, such as their own code.

OpenAI found this in February reported it as unauthenticated remote code execution that works in both directions, so a malicious client can take over an unpatched server and a malicious server can take over an unpatched client that accepts compressed responses.

The root cause was fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn't recognized as a security issue at the time and no release shipped with the fix until now. That means every project that bundles Brotli has to ship its own update. 

You’re exposed if any environment has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x installed, since HTTP clients such as requests, httpx, and aiohttp load these packages automatically when they’re present. Upgrade to Brotli 1.2.1 or brotlicffi 1.2.1.0 and rebuild any container images that bundle them. As of October 23, advisory databases don’t map the CVE to either PyPI package, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won’t flag vulnerable versions yet.

You can see what we’ve tracked here in Aikido Intel. 

As for unaffected software, Apache’s standard does not decode Brotli

How to patch HTTP2Shell CVE-2026-111497

For CVE-2026-111497, update the affected runtime or Brotli library:

  • upgrade to 22.23.4, 24.22.1, or 26.12.1, or a newer supported release in the corresponding release line.
  • Native Brotli / libbrotli: upgrade to . For older release lines, use patched or .
  • upgrade Brotli to and brotlicffi to , wherever installed.
  • update its Brotli dependency to , a patched older release, or the vendor’s security-fixed package. Bundled or statically linked copies require an updated application build.
  • upgrade to . Rebuild compiled executables that bundle Bun.
  • upgrade to 1.40.0, 1.39.3, 1.38.6, or 1.37.8, or a newer release in a supported branch. also includes the fix, but the 1.36 branch is unsupported.
  • the fix is included in 1.29.9, 1.30.6, and 1.31.2. Use a newer supported release in the corresponding line; the 1.29 branch is end of life.
  • Operating-system packages: install the vendor’s security update. Vendors may backport the fix without changing the upstream version number.
  • Other HTTP servers, reverse proxies, API gateways, and HTTP clients: update the affected runtime or Brotli library they use. Where Brotli is bundled into the product, install the product vendor’s release that explicitly addresses this CVE. For managed services, confirm remediation with the provider.

Update dependency locks, rebuild affected applications and container images, redeploy, and restart services. Verify that running workloads use the patched components.

Fixed releases, reviewed October 23, 2026
22.23.4 · 24.22.1 · 26.12.1Use a supported release line.
1.40.0 · 1.39.3 · 1.38.6 · 1.37.81.36.12 also includes the fix, but 1.36 is unsupported. Use a supported branch.
1.29 is end of life, so move to a supported line.
Choose the fixed release for your library branch.

What to do if you can't upgrade yet

These workarounds reduce exposure while you prepare the upgrade:

  • where Brotli support is optional, uninstall both Brotli and brotlicffi from affected environments. Remove dependency extras such as httpx[brotli] and any other requirements that would reinstall them, then regenerate dependency locks and rebuild/restart workloads. HTTPX, Requests, and urllib3 retain gzip and deflate support without these optional packages. However, a server that sends Brotli anyway may produce an unreadable response or an application error; automatic fallback is not guaranteed.
    • Uninstalling both Python packages and restarting workloads removes the decoding paths provided by those packages for incoming and outgoing data. It does not remove separate Brotli decoders bundled into other runtimes, libraries, or products.
  • reject requests whose Content-Encoding includes br at the reverse proxy, load balancer, or application middleware, before any vulnerable decoder processes the body. Match br case-insensitively, including within lists of encodings. 
  • remove br from Accept-Encoding. Also disable Brotli response decoding or reject responses whose Content-Encoding includes br before decoding begins. Ensure this check occurs before automatic body processing; checking after the client has downloaded and decoded the response is too late.

Changing Accept-Encoding alone is insufficient: a malicious server can send a Brotli response regardless of what the client advertises, and urllib3 selects its decoder from the response’s Content-Encoding header.

Keep these controls in place until affected components are patched and verified. Review coverage as vendors confirm additional affected components or attack paths.

How Aikido helps with CVE-2026-111497

Aikido flags vulnerable versions of Brotli and brotlicffi in your repositories, container images, and dependencies, including when they arrive as transitive dependencies. Your dashboard shows which services still run a vulnerable version, so you can upgrade the ones that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies first. 

Once you've upgraded, Aikido checks if the finding is gone.

Brotli is a widely used compression library from Google. On Wednesday, October 22nd NodeJS disclosed CVE-2026-111497, dubbed “node2shell,” wherein a Node.js process that decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data can be made to leak memory or run arbitrary code. Users were exposed if their app or a library decompresses bad Brotli data (e.g. the built-in fetch(), body-parser).

The next day, Python released a security update that patches the same flaw; Python packages were also vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497. Brotli flaw may affect even more languages and service applications, given how widely integrated the library is downstream. It turns out OpenAI had found this back in February.

Techincal details of CVE-2026-111497

The flaw sits in DecodeBlockTypeAndLength(), which handles block switches, the points where a Brotli stream changes which Huffman tree it uses. In vulnerable versions the function returns a plain boolean, and BROTLI_FALSE can mean either "this stream is malformed" or "I need more input." Callers can't tell the two apart, and on the fast path the decoder discards the return value entirely.

A crafted stream can declare a single block type and then exhaust that block's length, which forces a switch that can't succeed. The decoder then either reports that it needs more input for a stream that's complete, or keeps decoding with the block state it already had. That second path leads to the out-of-bounds write.

The upstream fix, google/brotli commit 0ed4268, makes the function return an error code and adds a new error, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH (-17). Decoding now stops on a format error on both the safe and fast paths. OSM diffed the Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 source distributions and found that 1.2.1 differs only in the version bump and the decoder changes from that commit.

Brotli vulnerabilities in Python libraries (CVE-2026-111497)

The Brotli flaw behind Node2Shell (CVE-2026-111497)  affects Python. Two PyPI packages, Brotli and brotlicffi, compile the same vulnerable Brotli decoder that Node.js bundles. An official advisory was posted on GitHub. Brotli has per month.

You're affected if any Python environment you run has Brotli 1.2.0 or earlier, or brotlicffi 1.2.0.x, installed. Popular HTTP clients such as requests and httpx load these packages automatically . Some packages automatically install Brotli as a dependency such as Scrapy, while others require explicit mention of it. An attacker can reach the vulnerable decoder by sending a malicious Brotli response to a request your app makes, or by sending your app a request body compressed with Brotli. That means an app can be exposed without importing Brotli anywhere in its own code. It’s a popular transitive dependency, so check your systems.

To fix it, upgrade to the patched releases:

    The release notes for both fixed versions don't mention the CVE. As of October 23, advisory databases don't map it to either PyPI package yet, so pip-audit, Dependabot, and Safety won't flag these versions.

    Who is affected by CVE-2026-111497 in Python?

    You’re affected if any of your Python environments have one of these packages installed:

    Your code doesn’t have to import either package. These HTTP clients advertise Accept-Encoding: br and decode Brotli responses automatically:

    • urllib3 (and therefore requests) when Brotli or brotlicffi is installed
    • httpx with the brotli extra
    • aiohttp when Brotli is installed
    • Scrapy, and anything built on the clients above

    Attacker data can reach the decoder through two routes:

    • Outbound requests. Your app fetches a Brotli response from a server an attacker controls, such as through a webhook delivery, URL preview, crawler or “fetch this URL” feature.
    • Inbound requests. Your framework or middleware decodes a request body sent with Content-Encoding: br, which is the Python equivalent of the Express 5 case in Node.js.

    How to fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python

    The fix is a package upgrade, and it takes four steps:

    1. Upgrade whichever package you have installed with pip install -U "Brotli>=1.2.1" or pip install -U "brotlicffi>=1.2.1.0". If you use a lockfile with Poetry, uv, or pip-tools, update the constraint and regenerate the lockfile.
    2. Rebuild your container images and any wheels that bundle either package. An image built on a vulnerable version stays vulnerable until you rebuild it.
    3. Check every environment you run, including laptops, CI runners, servers and containers. Many projects pull in Brotli through an HTTP client extra, so look at your full resolved dependency tree.
    4. Rely on a manual check for now. pip-audit, Dependabot and Safety won't report this until the advisory databases map the CVE to the PyPI packages.

    If your Python Brotli bindings came from a Linux distribution package instead of PyPI, the fix comes through your distribution, so check its security advisory as well.

    What is the Python Brotli vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497)?

    Python Brotli vulnerability refers to CVE-2026-111497, the Brotli decoder flaw known as Node2Shell, as it affects Python packages on PyPI. The CVE record pairs CWE-252 (unchecked return value) with CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).

    How serious is CVE-2026-111497 for Python, and is it being exploited?

    The CVE record gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, and Node.js rates it high severity. OSM built Brotli 1.2.0 and 1.2.1 with AddressSanitizer and ran a crafted stream through both. Version 1.2.0 consumed all of the roughly 23 MB stream and kept reporting that it needed more input, whether the stream arrived in one piece or in chunks as small as one byte. Version 1.2.1 rejected the stream with error -17 every time.

    OSM didn't pursue memory corruption or code execution in the Python extension. The decoder code is the same code that researchers exploited against an unmodified Node.js 24.22.0 build, as Imperva and others reported. For Node.js, The Hacker News reported no exploitation in the wild as of October 22.

    Treat it as urgent anyway. The bug is a memory-safety flaw in a component that handles untrusted network input, and the fix is a routine version bump. Services that call outside servers or accept compressed request bodies should go first.

    How to check if your Python app is exposed

    1. Check installed versions with pip show Brotli brotlicffi in each environment, and with docker run --rm <image> pip show Brotli brotlicffi for each container image.
    2. Find what pulls the packages in. Run pipdeptree -r -p Brotli to see which dependencies require it, and search your lockfiles with grep -i brotli poetry.lock uv.lock requirements*.txt.
    3. List the outbound HTTP calls that go to servers you don't control, and any endpoints that decode Content-Encoding: br request bodies.
    4. Upgrade the services that match step 3 first, then the rest.

    If you're reproducing the bug from Python, brotli.decompress() raises a generic brotli.error: decoder failed for any error, so you can't see which error code fired. A Decompressor() fed the crafted stream incrementally will never finish on 1.2.0.

    ‍Which versions fix CVE-2026-111497 in Python?

    Brotli 1.2.1 and brotlicffi 1.2.1.0, along with any newer releases.

    Do I need to import Brotli in my code to be affected?

    An installed package is enough. urllib3, requests, httpx and aiohttp use Brotli or brotlicffi automatically when either is present and decode Brotli responses from any server your app calls.

    Will pip-audit or Dependabot flag this?

    Not yet. As of October 23, the CVE record, OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database don't list either PyPI package. OSM is submitting PYSEC entries and a PyPI package mapping for the GitHub advisory so that tooling picks this up.

    Uninstalling Brotli and brotlicffi removes the vulnerable decoder, and HTTP clients fall back to gzip and deflate. Rejecting Brotli-encoded requests at the edge reduces inbound exposure, but it doesn't protect against Brotli responses your app fetches.

How Block Blast harvests its players for ad money
items.content:
I posted a video about this game that got over 15 million views, so I wanted to do the full technical write-up: the code, and how you can reproduce it yourself.

Some context on why it matters: between January and May 2026, Block Blast made an estimated $127 million from ads. Candy Crush Saga made $81.1 million over the same months (Sensor Tower estimates).

Most of Block Blast isn’t in the app you install

We started with the Android app, version 10.8.2. We decompiled the Java side with jadx and the native Cocos library with Ghidra, and found almost nothing interesting in the package you download from the store. Block Blast is built from small modules the code calls traits, and each trait has variants called arms. Running it on a clean Android 14 emulator with no account and watching its cache and logcat showed how it works: when the app launches, the server sends a config that says which arm of which trait you get, and the app downloads them as encrypted JavaScript. The config my install got names about 700 traits. My install selected 254 of them, and 101 were downloaded after install.

So two people playing side by side can be running different games, and the studio can change yours without an app update. Most of those 254 are ordinary: tutorials, animations, sounds. A handful are about when you lose. One of them is about ads.

The rule that waits for an expensive ad

It’s called RewardHighValueAdHarvestTrait. By finding where the game unlocks these files in its own native library, we decoded it into 15,616 bytes of plain, minified JavaScript. Its constructor sets the parameters:

It waits for three things to line up: you finished your last three rewarded ads, the ad loaded right now is worth at least 3.5 times your last one, and you’re 1,000 points past your high score. All three get checked in one function. Here it is with the minified null checks rewritten as optional chaining; the logic is the same:

Here’s how it checks each one.

1. You finished your last three rewarded ads. Every time a rewarded ad starts, the rule pushes onto a list and keeps the latest three (lines 174–183). If the ad SDK reports that the reward was earned, it flips that entry to (191–199). The check needs all three to be exactly :

That flag comes from AppLovin MAX’s callback in the Java layer, so an ad you close early stays .

2. The ad loaded right now is worth at least 3.5 times your last one. The rule reads the value of the best rewarded ad currently loaded with NativeAd.callNativeGetMaxEcpmNumber("2") (line 304). In the Java layer, that call goes through each ready rewarded ad slot, takes the revenue AppLovin MAX reports for it, multiplies it by 1,000, and returns the highest. The value of your last rewarded ad gets the same ×1,000 (line 310), so the comparison is like for like:

3. You’re past your old high score. At the start of each game the rule saves your high score (line 145). The bar is that high score plus (lines 107–110). Each player gets one arm: mine, , uses 1,000, and the app’s bundled config has others at 500 and 750. If you revive after the rule fires, the bar moves up another step, so it can fire again in the same game.

Then it asks for the lethal puzzle. Before dealing your next set, the game runs a list of “bottom offer” rules in order. When this one qualifies, it replaces the list with a single generator:

returns (line 102). The game sends that request to its puzzle engine and deals the three piece IDs it gets back (main script lines 45062–45121 and 15074–15123). If the engine fails to find a set, the rule resets and tries again on the next deal.

To watch it decide, we ran the downloaded file itself, unmodified, with test ad and score values. It requests the lethal puzzle exactly when all three conditions hold: 28 cases, including two ads instead of three, one ad closed early, a score 1 point short, and an ad worth just under 3.5×.

Then we ran it live, in a test copy of the iPhone app running in Apple’s simulator, and read the rule’s inputs while we played. It had three good rewarded ads on record. The score was past the line. A rewarded ad from Google AdMob was loaded and ready. The rule priced it at 72.39, against 37.41 for the last one, which is 1.94 times. It needs 3.5. So on iPhone the rule is live, reading real ad prices, and waiting for an ad worth 3.5 times your last one.

The name maps through three tables in the main script:

Algorithm 24001 exists twice: in JavaScript, and in the game’s native C++ library, where the function is called (their spelling). They do the same search. Here’s the JavaScript core:

It looks for two pieces that fit now and one that doesn’t, and keeps the set only if no order and no set of positions places all three, counting every line you’d clear along the way. Two of the three fit when they’re dealt, so the hand doesn’t look impossible until you try it.

Here’s what that looks like, with the game’s own code running in your browser. Step through it:

Press “New random board” for a fresh mid-game board, and the game’s code picks a new hand for it. On the test board in the evidence bundle, the game’s generator accepts a vertical domino, a horizontal domino and a 3×3 square as a lethal hand: we tried all 171 placements, and none of them finish it. On an empty board, those same three pieces fit 67,680 ways in each order.

The ad rule isn’t the only one that asks for it

The lethal puzzle is a generator, and any rule can ask for it. The ad rule is one caller. While we were testing it live on iPhone, a second caller fired on camera: . Once you’re 10% past your high score, it rolls on every deal, and 20% of the time it asks for the same lethal puzzle:

Our record was 1,304, so its line was 1,434. At 3,356 points it rolled, and the game dealt a five-long bar, a five-tall bar and a zigzag. The game’s own record of that deal names this rule as the caller, shows algorithm 9 both requested and used, and labels all three pieces 致死题, lethal puzzle. There was no way to place them. Two separate exhaustive searches agree: zero. The rule, the live settings and the deal are in the live iPhone bundle.

The model that picks where you lose

The rules so far are hand-written. The game also downloads trained models and runs them on your phone, and one of them decides where in a level the lethal puzzle shows up.

It’s a 500-tree XGBoost classifier for the game’s level mode, which the code calls Chapter. Its file is named predict_travel_difficulty_dead, and its 52 inputs are mostly about how you’ve been doing: your current level, how many times you’ve tried it, how many games you’ve finished this week, and how long you’ve had the app. The game feeds it 12 options, four values of a setting called times three difficulty levels, and keeps whichever one the model scores highest:

Another rule turns that pick into a stretch of the level: the first 30%, 30 to 80%, or the last 20%. When you reach that stretch, it offers you an extra revive if you usually take them (more than 75% of the time). Then, from the fourth deal after that, it asks for the lethal puzzle:

Other rules read the same pick the opposite way and make a level easier when it lands on the fourth option.

The model that prices you

A second model puts a price on you. The game downloads xgboost_regression_model111.json from its server and runs it on your phone.

It’s an XGBoost regression model: 59 decision trees, up to 8 levels deep, 27 inputs. Most of it is about money: 18 of the inputs are about the ads the game has loaded for you, today and yesterday. The rest are where you are, your phone, when you installed, and how your first game went. The trees lean hardest on your first score, the price of your latest ad, your RAM, your phone model and your country.

The code calls its answer . eCPM is the ad industry’s name for what a thousand ads are worth, and it’s the same unit the game stores its ad prices in. So the model is estimating what you’re worth in ads.

GPT-6 Astra ported the game’s input code and tree walk, and the port reproduces the game’s own outputs to the last decimal. We ran it on a made-up new player in the US with a first score of 1,000, once on an iPhone 15 installed from the App Store and once on Android, then changed one input at a time:

Nothing (US, first score 1,000)

Moving the same player from the US to Brazil cuts their value to about a third, and India cuts it further. Your first game matters too, but not in a straight line: on iPhone, a first score of 500 makes you worth more than 2,000 or 10,000.

The game uses prices like this to decide what kind of ads you get, and how many. The clearest case asks its server for two prices for you, one for full-screen ads and one for rewarded ads, and compares them:

In the versions the app ships, if your rewarded ads are worth at least twice your full-screen ads (1.5 or 2.5 times in other versions), you get an extra chance to revive, and a revive plays a rewarded ad. If full-screen ads pay more for you, you don’t.

Other rules work the same way. FullScreenAdAddByEcpmTrait adds an extra full-screen ad when your price is high. IsOpenEcpmTooLowNoInterTrait skips full-screen ads when you’re worth almost nothing. A few more open an early or a third revive when your rewarded ads are worth enough.

Try the on-phone model yourself:

Here’s the part of the game that walks the trees. It’s a plain loop: start at the root, go left or right on each input, add up the leaf weights.

A model that guesses you’ll play less tomorrow

There’s also a 1,000-tree LightGBM model with 93 inputs that predicts whether you’ll be less active tomorrow. It leans hardest on how long you’ve had the app, your high score, your RAM and your average score. If it scores you at 0.69 or above, a companion rule swaps in a pink revive button, and the revive skips the ad:

Some rules send your data out and act on the score that comes back, from server models with names like churn, LTV, revive-click and xDeepFM. Their weights stay on the server, so all we can show is what the phone sends. One of those requests, to , sends 40 fields, including your carrier, storage, the hour and stats on your recent ad prices.

Other rules that shape your game

The ad rule isn’t the only one that changes your pieces or your score. We caught one working live on iPhone. MaturityDevelopmentV2Trait gives each session a “maturity” score made of three parts: habit (10.98), skill (14.66) and your ad history (19.27). Ours added up to 44.91, under its line of 65, so it swapped some of the hard puzzles it would have dealt for easy fills. Another, , stepped in after two games below our record and asked for easier pieces.

These came up while tracing the ad rule on Android, and each has the same kind of evidence in my research files.

MultiClearBoostThenKillTraitSends your user ID to two server endpoints and gets back two labels. The code names both tiers as “not sensitive to being forced to die” (怼死不敏感). For those tiers, it waits for a big clear, then requests the lethal puzzle a few rounds later once the game has lasted about as long as your usual game.
A six-arm experiment on how soon the lethal puzzle can be requested: never, or after 4, 6, 10, about 17 or 30 minutes. For each arm it reports whether you started a new game within 15 minutes, and what share of revive offers you accepted.
Asks for hard pieces when your last six sets averaged under 4.2 seconds each and you’re past 93% of your high score.
After one kind of extra revive offer, adds a random bonus of up to 10% of your high score to your current score.

Is it the same on iPhone?

Yes. We took apart Block Blast for iPhone too, version 7.4.9, and a second GPT-6 Astra run checked those findings from scratch. It downloads the same rule from its own update server, and the file matches the Android one except for one line. Everything else is identical: three ads, 3.5×, the score bar, and the same lethal-puzzle generator.

The iPhone app also lists a second version of the rule, RewardHighValueAdHarvestV2Trait, and in that one the ad-history check can be switched off:

The app ships 12 versions of it. Half turn that check off, and they need anywhere from 1 to 3 ads, so in some of them a single rewarded ad you closed early is enough. The price bar depends on how long you’ve had the app: 3.2× the first ad loaded that session in your first week, 2.7× through day 30, and 3× your last ad after that.

What happens if I play without wifi?

This rule is saved on your phone after it downloads, so it still runs offline. But it only fires when a rewarded ad is loaded, and ads load over the internet, so once nothing is loaded it can’t fire. Other rules keep going. On my Android install, the one that asks for hard pieces when you’re playing fast near your record runs entirely on your phone. The one that asks the server which players “don’t mind being forced to die” can’t get an answer offline, so it stays off for that session.

Does an ad blocker do anything?

It depends on the blocker. Browser ad blockers, on iPhone or Android, only work inside the browser, so they don’t touch the game. A blocker that covers your whole phone, like Private DNS on Android or a DNS or VPN-based blocker on either, can stop rewarded ads from loading, and then this rule can’t fire, for the same reason as playing offline. The rules that don’t use ads keep running: the fast-play one, the experiment that times when the lethal puzzle can be requested, and, since you’re still online, the one that asks the server about you.

Is this why I always lose right after beating my high score?

That’s exactly where these rules are aimed. We caught doing it live: once you’re 10% past your record, every deal has a 20% chance of being the lethal puzzle. The ad rule waits for 1,000 points past your record (500 or 750 in other versions), and after a revive it moves the bar up and can fire again.

Not really. On Android, the original rule needs your last three rewarded ads to pay out, so closing one early does turn it off until you’ve had three good ones in a row again. But on iPhone, the V2 versions can skip that check completely and fire after a single ad, even one you closed. And the other rules that ask for the lethal puzzle, like the timing experiment and the one that waits for a big clear, don’t look at your ads at all. The one thing that stops this rule everywhere is not having a rewarded ad loaded, which is what happens offline or with a phone-wide ad blocker.

Isn’t this just adaptive difficulty?

Adaptive difficulty changes the pieces based on how you’re playing. This rule doesn’t look at how well you’re placing pieces. Its inputs are your recent ad results, the price of the ad sitting in memory, and your score relative to your record. And the generator it asks for isn’t a harder set of pieces. It’s a set chosen because no way of placing it works.

Is this even allowed? Doesn’t Apple review apps?

Apple reviews the app you download from the store, and this rule isn’t in it. The app downloads it from the game’s server after you install, and the server decides which players get which version. Apple does let apps download JavaScript updates like this, which is how tools like Expo Updates work, as long as the update doesn’t change what the app is. Whether changing your pieces based on ad prices fits that is up to Apple.

Why does it run on the phone instead of their servers?

The server does decide who gets the rule and which version. But the decision itself needs things only your phone knows in that moment: your board, the next set it’s about to deal, and the ad that’s loaded right now. So that part runs on the phone, which is also why it could be taken apart.

  • Android: the 10.8.2 XAPK from APKPure, downloaded October 11, 2026. All its split APKs pass signature verification, and the version matches the public listing on APKMirror. iOS: the 7.4.9 IPA from a public mirror. 4,670 of its game resources, including the main script and the catalog, check out against Apple’s code signature.
  • The rules came from their servers. The Android app’s cache says it downloaded the rule from , the same host it fetches all its traits from. We fetched that URL separately, and the file matched the app’s cached copy byte for byte. The iOS app’s signed catalog names both iOS rules, and the app fetches them from . As of October 15 all three URLs still serve the same files, so you can check this yourself (commands below).
  • It was assigned and loaded. On a fresh Android 14 emulator with no account, at 23:01:15 UTC on October 11, the app had the config ready, arm 332243014 selected for this rule, the module loaded with its storage initialized, and the bottom-offer pipeline it plugs into switched on.
  • The traits are encrypted with XXTEA and compressed with Brotli. The decoded rule’s hash is below. For the native library, my offline decode matched a memory dump of the running app across 25,317,680 bytes with zero mismatches.
  • Nothing in the Android game was changed. The only change was a rendering workaround so the game would draw on the emulator. No scores, ads, flags or config values were edited.

There are three evidence bundles: Android (113 KB, SHA-256 bd55151e6a1527f628459c2fffa115d5b14a765a3fb5a3f729387fbac6f707c8) and iOS (2.7 MB, SHA-256 02bdb0e0e9b02d77844efbcf4b82f48e17f2b688fc48cbf84f83e75ae289df7d), plus a third for the live iPhone catch (270 KB, SHA-256 5f36863daabd2b500c8062d005f41e6c5e7dcea5a238c89e558e19a928dcc57f). The Security Research Device (SRD) is a specially fused iPhone that allows you to perform iOS security research without having to bypass its security features. Apple Security Bounty — including bonus awards for preview and beta software programs.

items.title: Twelve years of distributed SQLite
items.content:
In September 2014 I published a short post announcingrqlite. The idea was simple: take SQLite, put a Raft log in front of it, and replicate every write to a cluster so that the loss of a node did not mean the loss of the data. The source went on GitHub that same weekend. As far as I can tell, that was the first open-source system to combine Raft and SQLite. Nobody else was doing it, and for several years nobody else tried.

Today “distributed SQLite” is a category with a dozen projects in it, a few of them venture-funded, two of them acquired. Since the people now writing about the category tend to start the story around 2021, I thought I should write down the version that starts in 2014. I was there for all of it.

The need was concrete. A clustered system I worked on at jut.io needed a small amount of relational storage, and the question of which node should hold it had no good answer. Replicating SQLite with a consensus protocol solved it. We went another way at work, but I kept building rqlite because the problem was general and the solution was small. The first version used goraft, the same library InfluxDB and etcd used at the time (I subsequently joined InfluxDB as a core developer around the same time). In early 2016 I replaced it withHashicorp’s Raft implementation which rqlite still uses.

The design decision that mattered most was made then and never changed. rqlite is a CP system. Writes must go through the leader, a majority must acknowledge, and a partitioned minority refuses writes. Everything else, the HTTP API, the read-consistency levels, the snapshotting, followed from that.

Before 2014, and alongside it

Two things deserve mention for honesty’s sake. Expensify had been replicating SQLite inside its own infrastructure for years with a Paxos-style protocol; they released it as Bedrock in 2016. And ActorDB, an Erlang system that gave each “actor” its own SQLite database replicated by Raft, appeared around the same time as rqlite. Neither was widely adopted outside its origin, but both show the idea was in the air. What rqlite did was make it a standalone, general-purpose, open-source thing anyone could run.

Canonical built dqlite to get LXD and later MicroK8s an embedded replicated store without running etcd. Mark Shuttleworth actually called me once, and we talked, hoping that rqlite could be made to work, but it never quite fit. dqlite began in Go and was rewritten in C with its own Raft library. It is the project most similar to rqlite in intent, and the main difference is of one of packaging: dqlite is a library you embed, rqlite is a server you run. Canonical’s need was a database inside their products: mine was a database beside anyone’s product.

2021: Litestream, and a change of approach

Ben Johnson (whom I worked with at InfluxDB) released Litestream in early 2021. Litestream does not use consensus at all. It watches the SQLite WAL and streams it to S3, giving you disaster recovery for a single-node SQLite database at almost no cost. Ben’s argument was that most applications do not need a cluster; they use one machine and need a way to recover if it dies. He was right about a great many applications, and the “SQLite is enough” movement of the next few years, with blog posts and conference talks, owes a lot to that argument.

Litestream and rqlite answer different questions. Litestream: what if the machine dies? rqlite: what if the machine dies and I cannot wait to restore? The first question is more common, the second is the one people have when they come to rqlite.

Fly.io hired Ben in 2022 and shipped LiteFS, which replicates SQLite at filesystem level with leases from Consul. It was the first attempt to make replicated SQLite a platform feature rather than a thing you deploy. And in a final twist, Litestream inspired rqlite’s v8.0 approach to handling the SQLite WAL.

2022: forks and extensions

Two projects in 2022 took approaches that neither rqlite nor Litestream had. cr-sqlite added CRDTs to SQLite as an extension, so that multiple writers could diverge and merge without a leader. That is the AP corner of the design space, and it suits local-first applications where rqlite’s CP guarantees would be a hindrance.

libSQL forked SQLite itself. ChiselStrike, later Turso, wanted to change things inside the engine that the SQLite project, which does not accept outside contributions, and would not change. On top of the fork they built a hosted service with replicas at the edge. Turso raised venture money on that, and in 2026 Supabase acquired them.

Around the same time, SQLite Cloud appeared, offering hosted SQLite replicated with Raft. It is the project closest to rqlite’s original design, wrapped in a cloud service.

2022 onward: the platforms

Cloudflare announced D1 in 2022, SQLite as a serverless database inside their edge network, and later put SQLite storage inside Durable Objects. This is replicated SQLite as a managed product from a company that does not need to tell you how it works. Turso’s service is the same shape. The category had gone from “a thing you run” to “a thing you buy.”

What the twelve years show

The core was right. SQLite as a storage engine, with replication added on the outside, has been reinvented by at least eight teams with different needs and different protocols. Nobody has found a reason to stop doing it.

The design space has three corners, and they appeared in order. Consensus first (rqlite, dqlite): one leader, strong consistency, a cluster. Streaming second (Litestream): one writer, cheap recovery, no cluster. Merge third (cr-sqlite, and parts of the local-first movement): many writers, eventual consistency. Each is correct for a different question, and most of the arguments are arguments between their users about which question is being asked.

And the money went to the platforms. rqlite, dqlite, and Litestream are open source and free. The projects that raised the capital or got acquired are the ones that turned replicated SQLite into a service with a bill. That is the usual fate of infrastructure ideas, and I do not mind it. But it is worth recording that the idea was open source for eight years before anyone sold it.

rqlite is still here. It does the same thing it did in 2014, a good deal better, and it is still the thing you reach for when you want a fault-tolerant relational database you can run yourself, understand fully, and not pay anyone for. Twelve years in, I am content with that position in the story.

We're introducing , the first model in our new K3.1 series and our most capable 3T-class open-weight model to date, with a 1-million-token context window. It delivers substantial improvements across coding, 3D creation, financial research, and other agentic capabilities.

We are also releasing , which delivers 2-3× the speed of K3.1 Pro for more responsive interactions.

Advancing the Frontier of Open Intelligence

Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.

Across coding, agentic, and knowledge benchmarks, K3.1 Pro matches or approaches the strongest proprietary models. On , which evaluates coding agents on realistic, resource-constrained terminal tasks using strict task-specific tests, K3.1 Pro scores 65.7%, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (58.2%) and narrowly behind Claude Opus 5.5 (66.4%). And on Kimi Code Bench 3.0 Long-horizon, our internal benchmark that tests coding agents' multi-step execution, tool use, and end-to-end problem solving across diverse engineering domains, K3.1 Pro scores , above K3's .

K3.1 Pro covers the full range of coding work, from quick fixes in real codebases to full-project builds. It also brings a more considered visual style to games and web experiences, and knows how to build them with the right tools.

K3.1 Pro works effectively across game engines such as Unity, Unreal Engine, and Godot, combining them with web search and 3D generation to create complete experiences. Its front-end pages, interactive Three.js scenes, and 3D assets show stronger composition, typography, animation, and polish. The examples below were created end to end by K3.1 Pro:

K3.1 Pro's long-horizon coding capabilities are also strengthened through large-scale reinforcement learning. In one internal test, it built a human walking dynamics simulator with integrated training and evaluation pipelines on top of , an open-source anatomical model of the human body comprising 296 skeletal components, including cartilage, and 402 muscle components. Across 167 missions and 420 independent reviews, it analyzed experimental results, diagnosed problems, and iteratively refined the walking controller, enabling the simulated human to go from collapsing within seconds to walking continuously with alternating strides for 11.2 seconds. When reward shaping failed to improve arm motion, K3.1 Pro did not simply keep adjusting the reward: it ran open-loop probes of the simulator's dynamics, identified and corrected 36 errors in shoulder-muscle moment-arm calculations, and then retrained the controller.

K3.1 Pro is strong at 3D creation and spatial reasoning. On , which tests 3D reconstruction from multi-view renderings through CAD code generation, K3.1 Pro scores 92.7% with tools, approaching the performance of and . From a text brief, sketch, or reference image, it can infer shape, proportions, and spatial relationships to create usable 3D models. It also has a stronger grasp of existing asset libraries and model collections.

K3.1 Pro particularly excels at parametric modeling, from mechanical parts and architectural models to configurable products and custom furniture. Without MCP connectors, it can write and run scripts for tools like Blender and CAD software to build and refine assets, edit components, and adjust geometry, materials, and scene layout.

Below are examples of 3D assets K3.1 Pro created for brand films, games, and interactive web experiences:

is now live on kimi.ai and the Kimi app — preview and edit your 3D models online, download them ready for 3D printing, or export them as videos or Live Photos to share anywhere.

With stronger reasoning and agentic capability, K3.1 Pro is capable of end-to-end delivery of complete financial workflows. K3.1 Pro achieves state-of-the-art results on OfficeQA Pro v2 (64.4), which tests complex fiscal data analysis over real financial documents through retrieval, cross-document verification, and multi-step numerical reasoning. K3.1 Pro also improves over K3 on Frontier Finance, which measures support for complete investment workflows from screening to profitability analysis.

K3.1 Pro also improves significantly across all our internal finance benchmarks:

  • evaluates formula linkage, financial logic, and final workbook quality in real-world modeling tasks. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 7.2 points.
  • evaluates whether models can produce auditable research under evidence and cutoff constraints. K3.1 Pro improves on K3 by 11.6 points.
  • evaluates long-horizon management and decision-making in a simulated business environment. K3.1 Pro achieves about 4.2× K3's performance.

Financial analysis and investment research demand a high degree of factual accuracy. To address this, we made targeted improvements to K3.1 Pro's on real-world tasks and challenging prompts. On Kimi Hallu Bench Hard bench, an internal benchmark designed to stress-test factual accuracy, its claim-level hallucination rate fell from 23.4% for K3 to 8.3%, while the share of responses containing at least one factual error was just 42.4% of its predecessor's rate. (The evaluation is a stress test for factual accuracy, with examples deliberately crafted to probe situations where models are prone to errors. The reported rates do not represent overall error rates in daily use.)

The cases below show how K3.1 Pro handles financial modeling, investment analysis, and source-grounded research in practice:

As K3.1 Pro became more capable, we spent a correspondingly larger share of our effort understanding where cyber capability comes from, and how much of it we can control. We therefore analyzed and evaluated K3.1 Pro's vulnerability research capabilities, and applied targeted controls during training to reduce potential misuse risk while preserving general usefulness.

Identifying and removing cyber-related data. During development, we observed vulnerability research performance improving steadily as post-training scaled. Tracing the source of this trend, we found that cyber-related content was embedded within the general mid-training corpus, and cyber-related tasks were present in the RL environment mix — a natural byproduct of training on broad data. In preliminary experiments on internal models, we found that without data removal at either the mid-training or the RL stage, downstream cyber capability would increase substantially. These findings gave us a concrete lever for control. For the open-weight release of K3.1 Pro, we identified and removed cyber-related data from both training stages, while retaining the general-purpose coding tasks needed for model usefulness. We will continue to apply appropriate controls at every training stage, of which cyber-related data identification and restriction is one example.

After data cleaning, we evaluated K3.1 Pro on xdev-bench-hard, our in-house benchmark of expert-curated, source-code-based vulnerability discovery and exploitation tasks, calibrated to provide meaningful differentiation at our current capability level. Most tasks faithfully reproduce recently disclosed vulnerabilities in software such as the Linux kernel, Node.js, JavaScriptCore, Exim, and VirGL, with mitigations enabled. Each task provides the vulnerable source code, a short bug hint, and the corresponding binary; the agent must develop an exploit, achieve arbitrary code execution in a separate sandbox, and retrieve a secret string for automated verification. We report pass@3 over a random subset of runs, with no hard timeouts or output token limits.

On xdev-bench-hard, the checkpoint without these risk-reduction measures — no cyber-related data removal at mid-training and no cyber-related RL environment filtering — solves 90.5% of problems at pass@3; the final K3.1 Pro reaches 81.0%. The comparison shows that data removal meaningfully reduces cyber capability relative to what the same training pipeline would otherwise produce. At the same time, K3.1 Pro improves substantially over its predecessor, indicating that stronger general coding and long-horizon debugging capabilities generalize to cyber tasks even after targeted data removal. K3.1 Pro's cyber capability remains behind that of frontier proprietary models that have been publicly available for at least three months. We will keep evolving our internal benchmarks so that evaluation stays informative as model capabilities continue to advance.

These evaluations frame our open-weight release decision. First, we aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability. K3.1 Pro's offensive cyber capability is, by design, below what our pipeline can produce, and remains behind that of frontier proprietary models. Second, we intend to progressively raise the cyber capability available in open weights. We believe making K3.1 Pro available in a non-discriminatory way benefits people who need dual-use capabilities for defensive purposes. When a capable model is open and runs on infrastructure its users control, many more teams gain the means to audit the code they maintain — including legacy systems that rarely receive dedicated security reviews. We believe that letting this capability diffuse gradually — rather than concentrating it in a few proprietary systems — ultimately makes all software more secure.

items.title: How to run a city builder on 16 MHz
items.content:
Do you feel spoiled by modern hardware? I know I do. Even the cheapest CPUs have at least 4 cores nowadays, running billions of operations per second. The idea that you could run any software on less than a GHz almost seems like fiction. Yet, there was a time when whole games ran at hardware a thousand times less powerful than that.

When thinking about impressive technical achievements in retro games, most people will first point to graphical milestones set by action games like Doom or Quake. Rightfully so, but at least I am personally far more impressed by the early examples of the city builder genre. Simulating whole economies on a large scale with a fraction of today’s power seems impossible if modern builder games even struggle on modern machines.

Of course this didn’t stop developers in the past to develop and run city builder games on significantly weaker hardware. The original SimCity for example lists Intel’s 386SX as the CPU in it’s system requirements. A CPU which at the time of it’s launch ran at magnificent 16 MHz.

(Note: an earlier version of this text mistakenly assumed that it ran on 12.5 MHz, which was the clock rate of base version of CPU, not the SX version. Whoops.)The idea of running a full game, especially one in the traditionally CPU-heavy genre of city builders? Pure magic from a modern point point of view.

So, why could Maxis run a full city simulation on this ancient hardware, when nowadays even simple idle games require multiple gigahertz of CPU power?

Of course there are a lot of reason for this, most of them external (OS ecosystem etc.) but this doesn’t mean that there are no clever optimizations done in the game code itself. Luckily, this source code was made public and released under the GPL license in 2008, under the name Micropolis. Don’t be confused by the name, this is still the code of the original name, but since only the code was made open source, not the trademark, it has to be called differently. But even under a different name, this is a precious resource, since we can exactly see how the game managed to run so well.

As is often the case when analyzing software performance, we can ignore 90 percent of the code. Our focus is on the core of the city simulation, the components that update systems such as traffic, fire, power, and crime.

And there is indeed one single function responsible for doing all of this: The Simulate() function in s_sim.c

As the comment implies, this function is called every frame and the function itself then calls the update functions of the various game systems, like CrimeScan(), FireAnalysis(), CollectTax etc.

The catch is that calling all those functions every frame would overwhelm our poor 1989 CPU. The solution: Not calling every function every frame.

Yep, SimCity just skips most of the simulation. Did you see the mod16 parameter of the Simulate function? Where you would normally expect a deltaTime? This number loops through the numbers 0 to 15 (you probably knew this already because of the name, didn’t you?), and is then used to decided which part of the simulation is run in this specific frame. The code for this looks something like this:

(Note: This is not the exact source, I removed some stuff to make it clearer for the explanation, but it’s veery close) .

So, obviously this makes the Simulation much faster to calculate, but how does this affect the gameplay? Well in case of SimCity, I would say barely. On average the simulation of an aspect takes 8 frames to react to the player’s action, 15 frames in the worst case. As an input lag for a shooter this would be obviously a disaster, but for the simulation of a city? I’d argue it might actually feel better than an instant reaction.

So far this optimization seems very specific for one kind of type of game, but actually it is the starting point for a lot of optimizations.Let’s look at another example, this time from Assetto Corsa (2014).

As a racing games one of it’s visual requirements is to render cars in a shiny way. To render those reflections the game uses the very common technique of regularity updated cubemaps. For a more detailed explanation what those are you can see my article on reflection rendering.

Since updating a whole cubemap every single frame would be a way to expensive task, the game uses a very similar trick as SimCity: It doesn’t update all 6 faces of the cubemap at once, but only a few, depending on the reflection quality setting.The settings UI doesn’t say so explicitly, but looking in the .ini file, we see the effect on the variable named FACES_PER_FRAME:

So far, we have stuck to the concept of distributing work across multiple frames by cutting longer tasks into fixed-size portions. For other tasks, it might be smarter to also determine the size and contents of those portions at runtime. For rendering tasks, this could be determined by factors such as screen size or the time since the last update. This explains why Unreal’s Lumen looks so good: It doesn’t need to recalculate all the lighting every frame. This is arguably also the reason why its results can look weird sometimes, for example, when reflections are not fully updated, like here:

Although such frame-distribution optimizations are most common in rendering code, I hope the SimCity example shows that they can work in other areas as well. The next time you work on gameplay code, ask yourself: “Do I really need to run all this code every frame?”

items.title: TornadoVM 7 Enables GPU-Native Workloads from Java Applications
items.content:
TornadoVM automatically accelerates Java programs on multi-core CPUs and GPUs. Rather than replacing existing JVMs, it works alongside them and provides a rich GPU programming ecosystem in Java that you can use with any mainstream JDK distribution such as OpenJDK, Graalvm, Temurin, or Zulu.

It offloads Java code to hardware backends, manages memory between the Java heap and accelerators, and runs the resulting compute kernels. This makes it a useful building block for modern cloud and machine learning workloads.

During development, TornadoVM compiles the source Java code to OpenCL and Apple Metal backends. The idea is that you can develop locally on your laptop and use the hardware available locally, and then deploy into a server that has Nvidia GPUs, and achieve major performance improvements - a form of "Write Once, Run Anywhere" for modern ML workloads.

Version 7 brings several architectural changes. The backends now use the Foreign Function & Memory (FFM) API in place of the Java Native Interface (JNI). The experimental JVM Compiler Interface (JVMCI) dependency has also been removed. According to the team, TornadoVM now sources "all compiler metadata through a reflection + ASM + Unsafe layer" which is the single, uniform path on every supported JDK (21, 25, 26 and 27).

The release also deepens integration with the Nvidia ecosystem through an optimized CUDA backend. This includes support for the cuTile programming model (via a new ) and the ability to call CUDA libraries such as cuBLAS and CUTLASS directly from within TornadoVM TaskGraphs. Developers can swap JIT-generated kernels for CUDA library calls, or chain the two together, depending on their performance and portability needs. Similarly, TornadoVM adds the same functionality for Apple's MXL library again via the hybrid API. Finally, support for multi-GPU execution has been added.

Not every Java computation benefits from offloading. The best candidates are data-parallel workloads, such as loops with no dependencies between iterations, because their iterations can run in parallel on the accelerator.

One of the goals of recent TornadoVM versions is to produce an idiomatic JVM environment for accessing the libraries that Nvidia have been tuning for different hardware platforms. The aim is for Java developers to tap into things like Linear Algebra, Fast Fourier Transforms (for Signal Analysis), Deep Neural Networks and hand-optimized matrix multiplication for sparse matrices. TornadoVM has library integrations with Quarkus, Lang4j, Flink, Spring AI and others and is also available through SDKMan.

For example, consider the integration of Apache Flink with TornadoVM - the main idea is that the developer writes a standard query as they normally would with the Table API. A configuration flag is used to indicate that this query should potentially be accelerated on a GPU.

Then, when the computation reaches the task manager, the framework checks if there is a GPU available in the node it is executing on and, if so, it connects to a library provider - which analyzes the intermediate representation (IR) of the query to see if the computation is actually suitable for GPU execution.

In total, TornadoVM offers four ways to program Nvidia GPUs as a Java programmer - Firstly, the parallel API which is really just an annotation that annotates a loop, and provides a hint for the compiler that this loop can be potentially paralyzed. This simple API did not prove to be sufficient in the long-term to get the desired performance for production applications, so additional APIs were added - such as the kernel context API and the already-mentioned TileContext.

Alongside the 7.3 release, the TornadoVM team introduced jitLLM v2.0, its next-generation Java AI inference engine built on TornadoVM. The team positions jitLLM as a direct competitor to llama.cpp and Ollama in performance, and it ships as a single JAR file.

Both TornadoVM and jitLLM are being commercialized through Beestream.ai, a spin-off founded by the TornadoVM team.

items.title: The Chalk and the Airplane
items.content:
“We are transitioning from an era of proof scarcity to proof abundance. For  thousands of years proofs were hard and… it required understanding and expertise and a bit of luck and talking to people and knowing the literature. It was universally valued because everyone who found a proof of a difficult theorem had to do all this difficult work and this helped grow the field. And now we found the shortcut. We found machines that can get these proofs for us and now we’re drowning in proofs, but we’re not getting all the understanding that we used to get.

“I guess we are seeing the end of the romantic era of mathematics — the age of heroes — which happened in other disciplines centuries ago as early as the industrial revolution. But somehow mathematics held on and we had our idiosyncratic traditions. For example, we all use blackboards, as you can see, and I’ve got this special Japanese-Korean chalk.”

    “My various PhD students and postdocs are in a state of total panic, and I understand them. And undergraduate, master’s, and bachelor’s studentsare also asking these same questions, quite simply. Is there a future for

    “[P]olicymakers will be making funding decisions in the coming years and we need to be ready to explain our added value. If people spend more time explaining that others are wrong and that their arguments are bad, we simply won’t have any arguments to present to these policymakers… I wrote this text for Proof Prompts… And I had this impression over the summer that there was a kind of imbalance in terms of speaking time and especially who was speaking, sometimes supporting the fact that AI was absolutely wonderful for math, and sometimes the fact that one could fear the consequences of this AI, or the use of AI… And so, I wrote a text that seemed quite measured to me… and I was surprised by the violence of the emails and messages I received following this text.”

    Would those policy decisions be effectual in such a situation? How can we explain “added value” adequately, when that value may not be realized for many years, or when the value (in a financial sense) of new learning may be unclear?

    Hearing this, the emperor promoted the old man for his loyalty across different environments. But in that example, the outcome is individual and not scalable. There is no emperor distributing boons for the mathematicians of today.

    “Seizing on that potential will require the careful integration of LLMs into the various STEM ecosystems, with the priorities of empowering a new generation of scientists, developing new STEM expertise, and preserving an open, collaborative, and intellectually independent scientific enterprise: that is the in the title. In the , scientific and technological output would still increase spectacularly in the short term, but, at the same time, independent human scientific activity would progressively weaken, the production of new knowledge becoming increasingly concentrated in a small number of hands, who become increasingly incapable of understanding the knowledge produced.”

    And in Quo Vadis, Mathematics?, we have the analogy of mathematicians as lone explorers navigating dangerous terrain on foot. Meanwhile airplanes come into common use, causing “disorientation, and a sudden loss of purpose. That grief is real, and I won’t pretend otherwise. But it will not last. Mathematics is about to graduate. It will grow into a full-scale industry and become the true infrastructure of all scientific and technological progress, a foundation that every other field stands on rather than a quiet corner of academia. The age of lone climbers is closing, and the age of mapping the whole continent is opening. As for me, I can’t wait to see those vast mountain ranges from my supersonic airplane.”

    That chalk that Tao mentioned must be supreme. A colleague of mine bought all he could when he learned that the original manufacturer was shutting down. But the blackboards are already gone.

My friend Joey got his face ripped off last week.

Yeah, while staring at his cheek in the mirror a few months back he noticed a a below the surface of his skin. Few months, few phone calls, few appointments later he found himself under the knife in a five-hour surgery getting a slowly untied and airlifted out of a in a high stakes game of .

Thankfully he’s okay and he’s all better and he’s managed to bounce over a pretty bumpy hill in life. We were all pretty nervous but he’s come out clean on the other side.

Plus, now he’s got a from his ear down to his neck to show for it.

And sure, over the years the stitches will drop out, hair might grow over, and the lines on his face could slowly fade away. But he’s really got a reminder of how lucky he is to be alive. He added some dents and scratches to his life story.

And unless you’re a ball of smooth skin and giggles, I’m betting your flesh and bones is covered with some scabs and stains, too.

Maybe it’s that fleshy scar on your hand from the eighth grade fistfight. You were on the bus back from shop class throwing around when tempers flared and a couple headlocks later you tripped and hit the ground.

Maybe it’s the ghost of that on your forehead. Did you squeeze it too hard before prom and end up with a bad cover-up job? If so, maybe you can still find your old friend in that photo album, wedged tightly between up-dos, , and freshly pressed tuxes.

Maybe it’s a you got with distant friends you don’t speak to anymore. You were young, you were graduating, you wanted a memento of getting through a tough year together. And you got it.

It’s the zippery line up your groin from the hernia, the tingly bump in your collarbone from the monkey bars, or the big on your back you’ve hidden under bathing suits for years.

But whatever yours are, , and however you got them, one thing’s for sure: your bumps and scratches are part of your life and part of your story. They’re part of your lows… and part of your glories. Yes, they’re memories of and reminders of good ones. And they all come together in a nicely wrapped package that we like to call… you.

See, we’re all a bit bent, we’re all a bit busted, we’re all a bit broken, we’re all bit rusted. Underneath all the crinkly jeans and beautifully personal collections of hairy legs, , and spotty skin.

So take a second to stop today and love all your scabs and patches. Just kiss those moles and and smile at all your scratches.
