items.content:
This is the ninth Godot tutorial in a series that covers the creation of procedural patterns on the GPU with shaders, using the Godot Engine, version 4.7. It follows Value Noise Derivatives and adds tiling to it.

Up to this point we have only considered value noise applied to a plane. Let's also take a look at how it gets applied to a torus. Create a scene like but with a material matching the one used in . Leave the displacement at its default 0.2 otherwise the torus will get too thick.

The torus has two obvious seams where UV coordinates 0 and 1 meet. We'll deal with that later. Let's first upgrade the bumpiness and frequency types to in so we can better tune them for the torus, like we did for the sine waves in the past.

uniform  bumpiness = 1.0;
uniform float displacement : hint_range(-1.0, 1.0) = 0.2;
uniform bool vertex_displacement = true;


#define USE_STANDARD_FRACTAL_PATTERN_SETTINGS

Adjust to work with the new frequency type.

PatternSample sample_value_noise(
		int octave,
		 frequency,
		vec2 uv,
		float time
) {
	…
	s.dx *= frequency;
	s.dy *= frequency;
	return s;
}

Now we have to reconfigure the plane scene, duplicating the old values for both components of the bumpiness and frequency. For the torus we again use (0.212, 0.637) for the bumpiness and let's set its base frequency to (6,4).

To make the pattern seamlessly wrap around the torus we'll have to tile it, so that it repeats itself for coordinates below 0 and above 1. To try this out we'll temporarily switch back to the plane. At the moment we've set UV coordinates to go from −0.5 to 0.5. We set the plane's base frequency to 4 with only a single octave and see what we get.

To test tiling we'll change the UV to go from −1 to 2 instead. Introduce a function that we use it both and so we only have to adjust the UV range in one place from now on.



void vertex() {
	if (vertex_displacement) {
		PatternSample pattern_sample = ;
		VERTEX += NORMAL * (pattern_sample.v * displacement);
	}
}

void fragment() {
	PatternSample pattern_sample = ;
	ALBEDO = colorize(pattern_sample.v);
	…
}

Because the usual UV range goes from 0 to 1 our goal is to tile the pattern in that UV range. That's the central tile in the middle of our plane right now. This tile is surrounded by eight tiles that are currently showing different patterns. When we're done all nine tiles in the 3×3 region should show the exact same pattern, without seams between them.

Tiling Lattice Coordinates

If we were using the hash noise pattern we could suffice with taking the fractional part of the UV coordinates and the pattern would tile perfectly. However, seams are part of the pattern so that provides no benefit. But value noise blends between adjacent lattice points, so we also have to blend across tile boundaries to eliminate the seams. This means that the lattice blocks at the tile boundaries must wrap their lattice points to match the opposite side of the tile.

For example, with frequency 4 the lattice coordinate sequence in one dimension is 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 for a single tile. Broken up into lattice blocks we get the lattice point pair sequence (0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,4). When tiling the end must wrap back to the beginning, so the coordinate sequence becomes 0, 1, 2, 3, 0 and the blocks become (0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,0).

Because we'll need to modify lattice coordinates we introduce a function that will use to get the first and second lattice coordinates for the lattice block in a single dimension. It takes the original lattice coordinate and returns it and the next one, which we'll locally name and . We return them packed in a . To perform tiling we'll also need to know the frequency.

Adapt to use this function.

	vec2 fractional_coordinates = sample_coordinates - lattice_coordinates;
	
	
	
	Hasher h = hasher(hash_seed + uint(octave));
	Hasher h0 = hasher(h, );
	Hasher h1 = hasher(h, );
	Hasher h00 = hasher(h0, );
	Hasher h10 = hasher(h1, );
	Hasher h01 = hasher(h0, );
	Hasher h11 = hasher(h1, );

Now we can start adjusting the coordinates in to repeat the pattern in the 3×3 block region that we're observing. Let's first consider negative coordinates. To make these match the central tile we have to modify them so they become positive, which we do by adding the frequency to .

	float l0 = lattice_coordinate;
	
	float l1 = l0 + 1.0;

This produces partial tiling on the negative side, along with a seam. To get rid of the seam we have to shift to the left side if it's on the right side of the tile, so when it ends up equal to or larger than the frequency.

	float l1 = l0 + 1.0;

This seamlessly tiles on the negative side, although it turns the tiles on the positive side into a mess. To fix those tiles we have to make the same adjustment to that we made to , if it didn't start out negative.

	float l0 = lattice_coordinate;
	if (l0 < 0.0) {
		l0 += frequency;
	}

Now we get perfect seamless tiling for the entire 3×3 region. However, it fails for larger regions, which becomes visible if we expand the visible region to 5×5.

This limitation is acceptable, because the goal is to seamlessly match UV coordinates 0 and 1. Our current cheap and simple approach supports this. It even works up to −1 and 2, so we can go at most one unit outside the 0–1 range. That allows for some wiggle room, for example for sliding animations, which we'll add later.

However, there is an additional limitation: the frequency must be a whole number so lattice points align with the tile edges. Otherwise the pattern will no longer tile.

Finally, tiling works with animation, but only when even frequencies are used. This is because we use staggered animation. If the frequency is odd then lattice blocks on opposite sides of the tile will use different time offsets for their matching lattice points.

Tiling usually isn't needed, so let's add a toggle option for it and disable it by default. It is also possible to add support for optional tiling per dimension, but we keep it simple and make it all-or-nothing deal. Let's also add some code documentation that explains the tiling ands its requirements, using a multiline comment in between . By adding a second to the opening statement the Godot editor's inspector will also display it as a tooltip for the shader parameter.

uniform uint hash_seed = 0u;

If tiling is disabled then we revert to the original approach in .

vec2 lattice01(float lattice_coordinate, float frequency) {
	
		float l0 = lattice_coordinate;
		if (l0 < 0.0) {
			l0 += frequency;
		}
		else if (l0 >= frequency) {
			l0 -= frequency;
		}
		float l1 = l0 + 1.0;
		if (l1 >= frequency) {
			l1 -= frequency;
		}
		return vec2(l0, l1);
	
}

With testing done we reduce the UV range back to a single unit. We won't subtract the old 0.5 offset anymore.

PatternSample sample_noise(vec2 uv) {
	return sample_fractal_pattern(
			standard_fractal_pattern_settings(),
			,
			TIME
	);
}

Now we can finally get a seamless value noise pattern wrapped around our torus. I increased the torus rings to 128 and its ring segments to 64 to make it smoother.

As stated earlier, tiling also works with animation as long as the frequencies of all octaves are even.

Let's wrap up by also adding support for sliding animation, which can make the animation of the torus look more interesting. Add a separate configuration option for a slide velocity.

uniform bool animation = true;

If animation is enabled use the slide velocity scaled by to offset the UV coordinates in .

PatternSample sample_noise(vec2 uv) {
	
	return sample_fractal_pattern(
			standard_fractal_pattern_settings(),
			uv,
			TIME
	);
}

This will quickly break tiling, because we go outside the supported UV region. So we have to limit the offset to a single unit at most, by only adding its fractional part to the UV coordinates. This ensures that we always stay inside the valid region.

		vec2 slide_offset = slide_velocity * TIME;
		
		uv += slide_offset;

items.title: C vs. C#: racing VLC's Gaussian blur
items.content:
Update, October 12: two small source changes bring the line-by-line C# within 8% of the C. Details at the end of Round 1.

In my last post, I showed that a native VLC 4 plugin can be written entirely in C#, thanks to .NET Native AOT. The obvious next question is not , but . VLC is written in C, video filters touch every pixel of every frame, and C# has a garbage collector. Surely that costs something?

Rather than guess, I picked a real VLC filter, ported it to C# line by line, and raced the two inside the same VLC, on the same frames, with byte-identical output. Then I optimized both and raced them again. Twice.

A Gaussian blur replaces every pixel with a weighted average of its neighbours: the closest count the most, and the weight fades along the bell curve Carl Friedrich Gauss used in 1809 to describe measurement errors. That smooth fade is what makes it look like an out-of-focus lens rather than a boxy smear. One number controls it, : VLC looks at neighbours up to 3 x sigma pixels away, so sigma 4 means a 25-pixel window.

It is one of the oldest effects in digital imaging: Photoshop 1.0 had it in 1990, and GIMP, FFmpeg and GStreamer all have one. VLC has had it since 2007, in Tools > Effects and Filters > Video Effects > Advanced, as “Spatial blur”:

A Gaussian blur is : blurring every row, then every column, gives exactly the same result as the full 2D window, so a 25 x 25 window (625 multiplications per pixel) becomes two passes of 25. VLC’s gaussianblur.c does exactly that, in integers: a horizontal pass into a buffer, a vertical pass over the buffer, then a division by the sum of the weights. Here is the horizontal pass:

The C# version is a deliberate line-by-line port: same loops, same bounds, same integer math, raw pointers where the C uses raw pointers.

It runs as a VLC plugin through VLCLR, compiled with Native AOT: a native DLL that VLC loads like any other plugin. The filter allocates nothing on the managed heap per frame, so the garbage collector has nothing to collect while it runs.

To keep things fair, every version below runs in the same VLC 4 release build, against that build’s own unmodified filter, and produces byte-identical frames to it. Each filter call is timed the same way, on a 1080p clip, on a laptop with an 11th-gen Intel Core i7 (Tiger Lake, 4 cores). Each round shows milliseconds per frame on .NET 10 at three blur strengths, next to frames per second at sigma 4. .NET 8 and 11 land within a few percent.

Milliseconds per 1080p frame (C# on .NET 10), lower is better.

C wins, as expected: the C# port takes about 23% longer per frame. Not a disaster, but a clear gap.

The machine code shows why. For the inner loop above, clang keeps the running sum in a register and computes the loop bound once. .NET’s code generator, RyuJIT, emits about twice as many instructions: it recomputes on every step and keeps the sum in memory. Same arithmetic, more bookkeeping around it.

After publishing, I checked how much of this gap is the code generator and how much is the way the C# is written. Two small edits close most of it: compute the loop bounds into locals before the loop, so RyuJIT stops re-evaluating on every step, and use for the indices, so they no longer need a 32 to 64-bit conversion before every memory access. Clang does both on its own. Same loops, same arithmetic, byte-identical output:

Milliseconds per 1080p frame (C# on .NET 10), lower is better. A new run, so the first two rows differ slightly from the table above.

With those two edits, the line-by-line C# lands within 8% of the C, and is ahead at sigma 4. Part of the gap was the compiler, and part was code the compiler needed a little help with.

Round 2: same algorithm, both optimized

Before reaching for SIMD, there is a lot to gain from the algorithm itself. I applied the same four changes to both, still plain scalar code with no SIMD and no threads:

  1. Replace the division by a multiplication. Away from the borders the divisor never changes, so a precomputed “magic” reciprocal and a shift give exactly the same result, without the slowest instruction in the loop.
  2. Read memory in the order it is stored. The vertical pass walked down columns, jumping a whole row ahead at every step. Accumulating whole rows instead reads memory sequentially.
  3. Use the symmetry of the bell curve. becomes : half the multiplications.
  4. Handle the borders separately, so the interior runs a simpler loop with no bounds to compute.

Milliseconds per 1080p frame (C# on .NET 10), lower is better.

The C# version, still plain scalar code, is 2.5 times faster than the current VLC code. C stays ahead, though: the C# takes about 24% longer, for the same reasons as in round 1. One more C advantage: clang turns these simpler loops into SIMD code by itself. I turned that off to compare the same code, but with it on, the C reaches 34 fps without a single line of SIMD in the source.

Round 3: tuned to the limit

The last round lets both sides use everything they have: AVX2 SIMD, on a single thread, with the same byte-identical output. C uses intrinsics from , C# uses System.Runtime.Intrinsics. The design is the same in both: 16 pixels per instruction in the horizontal pass, merged taps for the colour planes, and a division done exactly in floating point. The inner loop of the horizontal pass:

If anything, the C# better: the types say what is in each register, where C has one for everything.

In my first SIMD version, the C# took 14% longer, and 30% longer at the largest blur: same vector instructions, but clang unrolled the loops around them and kept their pointers in registers. So I kept going on both sides, with wider loops, two taps per multiply (), vectorized borders and no scalar tails. On the C# side only, I also reshaped the code until .NET produced what clang produces on its own: the hot loop in its own method, and weights broadcast straight from memory.

Milliseconds per 1080p frame (C# on .NET 10), lower is better.

Now it is close: at sigma 2 and 4 the two are on par, within the measurement noise, and the C# takes 9% longer at the largest blur. Both are 30 times faster than the current VLC code.

Current VLC code / line-by-line port
Same algorithm, optimized
Tuned to the limit (SIMD)
  • Line for line, the C# port takes about 23% longer. Not because of the garbage collector, which has nothing to collect here, or bounds checks, which raw pointers avoid. It is the code generator: LLVM does a better job on these loops than RyuJIT. two small edits that keep the loops and the arithmetic bring it within 8% of the C (see Round 1).
  • With work, the gap nearly closes. Part of that work was rewriting C# so .NET emits what clang emits by default. That is the real cost of choosing C# here: knowing what the compiler does with your loops.
  • C# is a realistic choice for a VLC plugin that does its work on the CPU. The C# filter blurs 1080p video at about 140 frames per second even at sigma 8, on one core.

Along the way, I also found two VLC bugs that have nothing to do with speed: with hardware decoding, any CPU filter turned half the picture green, and the blur reads two bytes past the right edge of each line. I’ve opened merge requests for both.

There are ways to make both versions faster still, such as AVX-512 or spreading the work over several cores, but I stopped there.

I would also like to know how much of the line-by-line gap really is the code generator. .NET has an experimental NativeAOT-LLVM branch that compiles C# with LLVM, the same backend clang uses. It only targets WebAssembly for now, so it can build a VLC plugin for the WebAssembly version of VLC but not for the desktop VLC used here.

This was an experiment to compare the two languages on the same CPU code, not the best way to blur video: a filter like this belongs on the GPU, and GPU versions of a few VLC filters are in progress.

If the last 10% matters, C is still the answer. For everything else, the language you are most productive in, plus a good algorithm, will get you further.

The blur is now part of VLCLR, in a new library: runs all of these versions on VLC pictures. The GaussianBlur sample wraps it in a complete VLC filter plugin of about 70 lines, from reading the sigma option to allocating the output picture.

As with the previous post, I designed the experiment and the rules, and Claude wrote most of the code and the benchmark harness.

items.title: Bringing uv and ty together
items.content:
Experimental uv-ty integration is now available, enabling first-class support for Python scripts (on the CLI and in the editor) and a unified command.

This is a step towards an integrated Astral toolchain, one that uses a shared understanding of your project to enable entirely new capabilities.

At Astral, we build high-performance tools for the Python ecosystem: uv, our package manager; Ruff, our linter and formatter; and ty, our type checker and language server.

Historically, each Astral tool has focused on making a different component of Python development more productive. But we see an opportunity to further Python by unifying traditionally separate capabilities into an integrated toolchain.

Our vision for the Astral toolchain is simple: while each tool should be individually usable, useful, and interoperable with the rest of the ecosystem, they should be even more capable when used together.

Today, we’re announcing an experimental integration between uv and ty, available in preview. uv understands your Python project’s environment and dependencies, while ty understands your code. By combining the two, we can unlock new functionality beyond what either tool can provide individually.

First-class support for Python scripts#

PEP 723 enables Python scripts to declare their dependencies and Python version requirements through inline metadata. uv already uses this metadata to prepare an environment when running a script. Now, ty can use this metadata to understand your scripts.

On both the command line and in the editor, ty now uses inline metadata to discover scripts throughout your project and leverages uv to prepare an environment for each script. These environments allow ty to check your scripts against their declared requirements.

Scripts can have different requirements within the same repository. Each script is checked against its own dependency declarations, even if those dependencies or Python requirements differ from the surrounding project.

Declare dependencies inline with PEP 723, save to sync with uv, and use ty’s completions, hover information, and Go to Definition capabilities in your editor.

Declare dependencies inline with PEP 723, save to sync with uv, and use ty’s completions, hover information, and Go to Definition capabilities in your editor.

When the integration is enabled in your editor, ty automatically invokes uv to prepare the script’s environment in the background, which it uses to provide type checking, code navigation, and completions based on the script’s declared requirements.

Over time, we plan to enable script support by default, and enable automatic environment setup for standard Python projects.

A unified checking command#

introduces a unified diagnostic interface to uv, starting with support for ty. Over time, we plan to support Ruff in to unify linting and type checking into a single command.

Running will automatically prepare your project’s environment, install the required dependencies, and check your project with ty. It “just works.” (If you never run , nothing changes for your uv experience; the ty binary is installed separately on first invocation.)

With , you can check individual packages, or an entire workspace. In a workspace, use uv check --package <name> to select an individual package, or to check every package. uv uses your workspace configuration to determine what to check, so the command stays the same as your workspace grows.

Sync your project’s dependencies and type-check your code with a single command.

Sync your project’s dependencies and type-check your code with a single command.

Standalone PEP 723 scripts have independent environments and are checked separately. Use uv check --script example.py to check a script using its declared requirements.

automatically uses the ty version recorded in your project’s lockfile. Commit your project configuration and lockfile, and developers and CI running will share the same ty version without separately maintained pins.

The ty pre-commit hook also uses under the hood to run ty before each commit over your Python project. By using , the hook automatically sets up the environment for ty from your project’s dependency declarations.

The uv-ty integration is powered by , which gives ty a structured view of your project or script’s packages, dependencies, and Python environment. ty then uses this information to provide type checking and editor features that reflect the configured environment.

For PEP 723 scripts, ty invokes uv to prepare the script’s environment, which includes installing declared dependencies. As dependency installation can require execution of third-party Python code, automatic environment setup is currently opt-in.

You can also check your project and its PEP 723 scripts from the command line with:

Running enables the integration automatically and requires no additional configuration.

Support for PEP 723 scripts and the command requires uv 0.12.3 or later, and ty 0.0.76 or later.

This integration is experimental, and we’d love your feedback as we refine the experience.

While this initial support largely leverages uv’s environment capabilities to power ty execution, we’re also working on a new category of checks that combine uv’s knowledge of your project’s dependencies with ty’s understanding of your code (e.g., to detect unused dependencies), which we’ll cover in a future post.

And, in parallel, we’re continuing toward ty’s stable release.

Thank you for building with us!

items.title: A practical guide to AI image generation, from diffusion to agents
items.content:
This is my general guide to AI image generation. It covers how the models work at a high level, the different types, a bit of history, what you actually get from ChatGPT and how to build image generation into your own code and agents.

It’s based on my own experiments calling a handful of image providers from Python. I’ve generated pixel art sprites, photorealistic card table backgrounds and a series of restaurant posters, trying to make one that doesn’t look AI generated. Every image here came from those experiments.

  • Most models start from noise and clean it up. Text steers the clean-up. Newer models also plan the image the way a chat model plans a sentence.
  • You pay for the canvas, not the content. A plain wooden table costs the same as a detailed oil painting of the same size.
  • ChatGPT is the easiest way in and the hardest to control. Great for one-off images and conversational edits. For anything repeatable you want the API.
  • Prices vary more than 100 times over. Anything from a fraction of a cent to 15 cents or more per image. Running a model locally costs nothing. The cheapest model isn’t always the cheapest result.
  • Models get retired with weeks of notice and providers quietly ignore parameters. Keep the model in config and log what you actually got back.
  • Describe how it was made, not how it should look. Camera, film, print process and layout get better results than “stunning” and “hyper-detailed”.
  • Spelling and fingers are no longer the giveaway. The tell now is taste. Too much glow, too much drama and nothing allowed to be plain.
  • A multimodal agent can write the prompt, call the API, look at the result and try again. You still need to supply the taste.
  • The best pipelines are hybrids. Let AI do the creative part. Let ordinary code do the exact parts like sizing, transparency, palettes and layout.
  • Ian Goodfellow’s generative adversarial networks pit two networks against each other, one making images and one spotting fakes. They go on to produce convincing synthetic faces but are hard to steer with text.
  • OpenAI links text and images in one model. You can type a sentence and get a picture, even if it’s a small, blurry one.
  • 2022 - The breakout year. DALL-E 2, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion all arrive within a few months. Stable Diffusion is open source and runs on a gaming PC with about 7GB of video memory, which kicks off a huge community of fine-tunes and tools.
  • 2023 - Photorealism and readable text. A Midjourney image of the Pope in a white puffer jacket fools much of the internet. Ideogram launches with text you can actually read. SDXL raises the bar for open models and DALL-E 3 moves into ChatGPT.
  • 2024 - Flux and the backlash. Former Stable Diffusion researchers found Black Forest Labs and release Flux, which becomes the default open-weight model. Meanwhile AI posters become a byword for cutting corners (more on that below).
  • 2025 - Native image models. OpenAI builds image generation into GPT-4o itself and the “Studio Ghibli” trend takes over social media. Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, nicknamed Nano Banana, makes conversational editing cheap at $0.039 an image.
  • 2026 - Abundance and churn. OpenAI switches off DALL-E in its API. OpenRouter alone lists over 60 image models from a dozen companies, and older models are retired every few months.

Six fingers and gibberish text

For a few years the easiest way to spot an AI image was to count the fingers or try to read the sign in the background. Both problems are now mostly fixed, and why they happened says a lot about how these models work.

are complicated, flexible and usually partly hidden in photos. Behind a cup, in a pocket, half out of frame. The models learned what hands look like as a texture, not how many fingers they have. Midjourney v5 in March 2023 was widely reported as the turning point. Experts suspected better curated training data with clearer pictures of hands, plus bigger models and higher resolutions. It wasn’t perfect. People in the background still had alien anatomy for a while.

had a more specific cause. Most models read your prompt through a tokeniser that splits it into chunks of words rather than letters. The model never sees that “chocolate” is spelled c-h-o-c-o-l-a-t-e, so it can’t draw it letter by letter. A 2022 paper, Character-Aware Models Improve Visual Text Rendering, showed that giving the model access to individual characters fixed much of the problem. Ideogram, whose team included former Google Imagen researchers, made text a selling point in 2023. By 2025 the multimodal models from OpenAI and Google, which understand language as well as any chatbot, had made readable text normal.

The fix arrived in stages, and the old problem leaked into the real world in between. The Willy’s Chocolate Experience in Glasgow in February 2024 promised “a pasadise of sweet teats” on its AI-generated posters. Long text is still not completely solved. In December 2025 Nano Banana Pro turned “Lived experience” into Liver experience on an otherwise good infographic.

You don’t need the maths to use these models well. You do need a rough picture of what’s going on, because it explains most of the surprises.

Most image models are diffusion models. During training they learn to remove noise from images. Take a photo, add a bit of static and teach the model to predict what the clean version looked like. Repeat billions of times at every level of noise.

To generate, you run that in reverse. Start from pure static and remove a little noise at a time over a number of steps. A text encoder turns your prompt into numbers that steer each step towards an image that matches it.

Two details matter in practice.

  • They work in a compressed space.Latent diffusion, the approach behind Stable Diffusion, paints on an internal canvas about 8 times smaller on each side than the final image, then decodes it. That’s why you can’t ask for a 32 x 32 image. The internal canvas would be 4 x 4.
  • More steps is slower and usually better, up to a point. “Distilled” models like Flux Schnell and SDXL Turbo are trained to get a good image in 4 steps instead of 30.

The newer approach puts image generation inside a model that also understands language. Because the same model reads your prompt and makes the picture, these are much better at following instructions, rendering text and editing an image you give them. GPT Image, Gemini’s image models and Meta’s Muse work this way. Some reason about the layout before they draw, which makes a real difference when the prompt is about where things go.

Are multimodal models diffusion under the hood?

Often partly, and the line is blurrier than the marketing suggests.

OpenAI’s launch post for GPT-4o image generation hints at a hybrid. A language model plans the image as a sequence of tokens, the same way it writes a sentence, and a diffusion-style decoder paints the final pixels. Google hasn’t published how its Gemini image models work. Going the other way, modern “diffusion” models like Flux use transformer blocks that process text and image together, which is the same building block as a chat model.

So the useful distinction isn’t the maths. It’s how deeply the image model understands language. That’s what gives you instruction following, readable text and editing.

Diffusion models (Flux, SDXL, Imagen)Multimodal models (GPT Image, Gemini, Muse)
Resolution and number of stepsImage tokens, usually fixed per size and quality tier
Cheap, fast, runs locally, seeds give repeatable resultsFollows instructions, renders text, edits from a reference image
Takes prompts more literallyOften no seed control and a fixed output size

The random static a diffusion model starts from is set by a seed. Same seed, same prompt and same model gives the same image. That’s what makes batches repeatable. Many hosted models ignore or reject seeds, so don’t build anything that depends on them without checking.

Types of image generation

“Image generation” covers several different jobs. Most providers support some of them, not all.

A prompt becomes a pictureConcept art, backgrounds, placeholders
“Make the mug blue” on an existing imageIterating on a design without starting again
Keep a character, product or style consistentThe same knight in eight poses
Teach an open model a new style or subjectA consistent house style or product
Add detail at a higher resolutionFinishing the keepers from a cheap batch
Transparent sprites and product shots
Produce SVG instead of pixels

Tileable textures are worth a special mention. Plain models won’t reliably produce a seamless tile. You need a model or LoRA trained for it or a tiling option in the tool.

One-off images, quick editsLittle control, usage limits
Midjourney, Adobe Firefly, CanvaDesigners, polished resultsSubscriptions, hard to automate
OpenAI, Google Gemini and Vertex AI
Free bulk generation, full controlNeeds a decent GPU or Apple Silicon, slower

For my experiments I deliberately avoided subscriptions. Everything was pay per image through an API or was run locally.

What you get with ChatGPT

Most people’s first experience of AI images is typing a request into ChatGPT. It’s worth knowing what you’re getting.

ChatGPT uses OpenAI’s own GPT Image models, which have been built into the chat since March 2025.

Not really. DALL-E 3 was ChatGPT’s image generator from October 2023 until the switch to GPT-4o image generation in March 2025. OpenAI then removed DALL-E 2 and 3 from its API on 12 May 2026. The name lives on mostly as a generic term for AI images.

  • You can say “warmer light” or “move the mug to the left” and it edits rather than starting again.
  • It handles layouts, counts and specific details better than older diffusion models.
  • Signs, posters and labels are usually spelled correctly.
  • Upload a photo or sketch and it will work from it.
  • You get a handful of aspect ratios, no seed and no way to run a batch. You can’t ask for exactly 1024 x 512.
  • Each image takes anything from a few seconds to over a minute, and there are usage limits, especially on the free plan.
  • Left to itself it drifts towards a recognisable look. The 2025 model was known for a warm yellow cast nicknamed the “piss filter”. Describe the lighting and colour you want rather than leaving it to the defaults.
  • It will refuse some requests, like real public figures in certain contexts or close copies of copyrighted characters.

OpenAI adds both C2PA metadata and a SynthID watermark to its images, according to its help centre. Google adds SynthID to Gemini images. Metadata is easily stripped. Watermarks survive screenshots better, but neither is something to rely on if you’re trying to prove an image is or isn’t AI.

The same family of models is available through OpenAI’s API, billed per image. The API gives you sizes from a fixed list, quality tiers, batching from code and, on some models, transparent backgrounds. If you need more than a few images or the same kind of image repeatedly, use the API. The Gemini app versus the Gemini API is the same story.

The most useful mental model I’ve found is a painter who only owns large canvases, charges per canvas and paints every square inch with the same care. A flat blue sky gets as much effort as a face.

  • Simple pictures aren’t cheaper. The model does the same work across the whole image.
  • You can’t generate small. Models work best at roughly 512 to 1600 pixels. For a 32 x 32 sprite you generate a big picture and shrink it yourself.
  • Asking for a smaller size often doesn’t help. Gemini 2.5 Flash Image returned 1024 x 1024 when I asked for 512 x 512, at the same flat price.
Does making it smaller help?
Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, Recraft
Per image, tiered by size and qualityNewer Gemini models, OpenAI GPT ImageA little. The smallest tier is still a big canvas for most needs
Per megapixel or GPU-secondReplicate, fal.ai, most models on OpenRouter
Yes, and speed is what you save

The landscape in October 2026

Prompt iteration and bulk batches
Flux Schnell on Replicate or fal.ai
Recraft V4.1 Flash (OpenRouter)
FLUX 3 Image Klein (OpenRouter)
Meta Muse Image (OpenRouter)Following layout instructions
$0.009 low, $0.034 medium, $0.133 highQuality tiers from OpenAI
~$0.039, half that via the Batch APIEdits and character consistency
Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image)~$0.045 at 0.5K, ~$0.067 at 1KNewer and better, but pricier
Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image)

Newer flagship models cost more per image, not less. The cheap end of the market is open-weight models and the “flash”, “mini” and “lite” tiers. OpenRouter’s model list is the easiest place to compare current prices.

Price per image is misleading on its own.

cost per usable image = (price per image x attempts needed) + your time

A free local model that needs ten tries can lose to a $0.039 model that gets it right first time. In my experiments a model costing a tenth of a cent more saved several retries.

Describe the camera, not the view

I wanted card table backgrounds for a game. That meant a table seen from directly above, with a few props around the edges and the middle kept clear for the cards.

Asking for “seen from directly above” isn’t enough. Models learn from photos, and most photos of tables are taken at an angle. My first attempts came back as nice pictures of a table with a wall and a window behind it, and every prop bunched down one side.

Two changes fixed most of it.

  1. “An orthographic flat lay. The camera points straight down at the tabletop, with no perspective and no horizon. The table surface fills the entire frame edge to edge. No walls, windows, floor or table edges are visible.”
  2. Spell out where things go. “Spread these around all four edges (top, bottom, left and right) rather than bunching them on one side or in the corners. Each one should be small and cut off by the edge of the image.”

Here’s the same prompt for a pine kitchen table, with both changes, run on two different models.

Both are now top-down. Flux leaves the props whole and pushes them into the corners. Muse, a multimodal model that plans before it draws, put one item on each edge, cropped each one and left the middle clear.

Marketing is where AI images get the most criticism

Posters, flyers and infographics are one of the most common uses for AI images. They’re also where it most often looks cheap.

  • The Willy’s Chocolate Experience posters promised “catgacating” and “exarserdray”. The event itself was so far from the pictures that people called the police.
  • A24’s AI-generated posters for drew criticism in April 2024. They showed scenes that weren’t in the film and had obvious errors, like a Chicago landmark rebuilt at the wrong angle. A lot of the anger was about a studio using AI instead of paying artists.
  • Karen Spinner’s experiment turning a research paper into an infographic is a great example with all the prompts and source material shown. It ended up “basically usable”, but only after six attempts. Along the way the model misspelled words, ignored instructions about white space and filled every gap it could find. Her advice was to keep the copy short and proofread everything.

Making a poster that doesn’t look AI generated

So I set myself a challenge. Could I get a restaurant poster that wouldn’t immediately read as AI?

My first attempt was a screenprinted trattoria poster. Rather than describe a look, I described a real print process. Three flat spot inks on uncoated paper, slight misregistration, a scan rather than a photo, an off-centre composition and a named design tradition.

The ink texture is convincing. The bottom line looks like clean digital type but the fold crease may be too much.

The harder test was a 90s burger poster with food that looks real. AI food tends to be too perfect, too glossy and too heroic. I asked for 1996 medium-format film photography and deliberately imperfect food, like a lopsided bun and pale winter tomatoes.

The first version had good food but read as a “vintage” filter, with comic lettering and fake wear. A real 1996 poster would have been clean and corporate.

So I made it boring. A pristine scan, a flat red background with an early-Photoshop gradient, a cut-out product photo with a slightly too-even drop shadow and plain heavy italic type. I even asked for it to look “competent and slightly bland”. That one would pass a casual glance. It isn’t quite 1996, because the shake is in a dome-lid cup you’d see in the 2010s.

For balance, I asked for the worst version I could think of. Unreal Engine, volumetric god rays, floating ingredients and a galaxy. It delivered a dozen patties with no bottom bun, a shake with no glass and fries raining down from space. Unlike AI posters of old (2 years ago), the spelling is correct these days. The giveaway now isn’t the spelling. It’s that every element is turned up to the maximum.

  • Describe how it was made. Camera position, lens, film stock, lighting setup, print process and scanning give the model concrete constraints.
  • Leave out the hype words. “Stunning”, “hyper-detailed” and “8K” push the model straight into the AI look.
  • Say what fills the frame, what’s visible and where each element goes.
  • Real design is restrained. Asking for “slightly bland” did more than any amount of detail.
  • Keep text short and exact. Put it in quotes, add “spell every word exactly as written” and proofread the result.
  • The model drifts towards modern objects unless you name the old ones.
  • Variants of the same prompt often differ a lot, and at a cent each, it’s cheaper than rewriting the prompt.
  • Lock in a template for batches. Use the same style suffix and seed for every asset in a category so the batch doesn’t drift.

Pixel art and game sprites look like the easiest possible job for an image model. Small, simple, few colours. They turn out to be a great example of how AI image generation is harder than you would expect.

A pixel art knight on Gemini 2.5 Flash Image took 7.5 seconds and cost about $0.039. It’s clean and convincingly retro.

But it’s a 1024 x 1024 picture of a sprite, not a sprite. The “pixels” wobble in size, don’t sit on a true grid and use far more colours than a real palette. The “solid” magenta background was a slightly varying pink. To make it usable I still had to remove the background, snap it to a grid with nearest-neighbour downscaling and reduce the palette, all in ordinary code.

Many sprites on one canvas

If you pay per canvas and a sprite only needs a fraction of it, the obvious move is to ask for many sprites in one image. It’s cheaper and more consistent, because the model draws everything at once with the same palette and lighting.

For a set of different objects it works brilliantly. I asked for 100 fantasy inventory icons and got 156, about 140 of them distinct, for one $0.039 call. That’s about $0.00025 per icon. Ordinary code then slices them by shape, removes the background and repacks them on a clean grid.

For one character in many poses it falls apart quickly. A 4 x 4 grid gave me about 13 distinct poses of the same knight. Asking for 10 x 10 gave me the same knight stamped 120 times.

Here is what I learned from seven calls and about $0.27.

  • The sweet spot is about 10 x 10 for sets of objects and 4 x 4 for character poses. Asking for more reduced both variety and quality.
  • The model picks the grid, not you. I asked for 8 x 8 and got 6 x 6. Never slice on a fixed grid. Find sprites by shape.
  • Scale everything together. If each sprite is resized to fill its own cell, a character grows and shrinks between animation frames.

What I did was a basic experiment with general models. If you need pixel art (a very specific type of image generation), there are better routes.

PixelLab is built for game developers. It draws real sprites at their actual size rather than a large picture that looks like pixel art. Palette, outline, camera angle and transparency are settings rather than prompt wording, and it can animate and rotate a character. It’s a subscription, so I didn’t use it here. Retro Diffusion is a similar commercial option.

To do it yourself, use a model add-on trained for pixel art such as Pixel Art XL, then shrink the result onto a clean grid and fix the palette in code. PixelOE can also turn any image into pixel art without AI. That works well for still images. Consistent animation is where the commercial tools are still ahead.

Vectors are another format that looks easier than it is. An LLM can write SVG code cheaply, but characters come out crude because it’s describing a picture without seeing it. Dedicated text-to-vector models like Recraft look much better but cost more than raster images.

The general lesson from pixel art is that AI is good at “what should this look like?” and bad at “put exactly this in exactly this cell”. What matters isn’t how simple the output looks. It’s whether the hard part is creative or structural. Use the model for the creative part and code for the structure.

Integrating image generation into a coding project

Put a thin interface in front of every provider

Every API is different. OpenAI has an images endpoint. Gemini returns images inside a chat-style response. OpenRouter has two endpoints depending on the model. Local Flux is a Python library or a command line tool. Hide all of that behind one function so switching provider is a config change.

Keep each provider’s quirks inside its own module. Base64 decoding, odd parameter names and fallback endpoints don’t belong in your app code.

Expect the ground to move

These all happened to me within a few months.

  • The Flux 2 models I planned to use vanished from OpenRouter between planning and building. Imagen 4 was shut down on the Gemini API. Gemini 2.5 Flash Image and gpt-image-1 got retirement dates, some with only weeks of notice. The Gemini deprecations page is worth bookmarking.
  • OpenRouter moved dedicated image models to a separate endpoint. Calling them the old way returns a 404. My code now tries one and falls back to the other.
  • Parameters were ignored or rejected. Gemini ignored size and seed. OpenAI snaps to the nearest of a few fixed sizes. FLUX 3 Klein rejects a seed outright. Muse returned 1600 x 1600 when I asked for 1024 x 1024.

So keep the provider and model in config, never in code. Check the size and format of what came back rather than trusting what you asked for. Run a scheduled smoke test against each provider so you hear about a retirement before your users do.

Record the prompt, model, parameters, output size, duration and cost for every image. Cost reporting is inconsistent. OpenRouter returns the billed amount. OpenAI and Gemini return token counts and leave the maths to you. Some return nothing. Without your own logging you only find out what you spent from the monthly bill.

Keeping the prompt and parameters with each image also means you can reproduce or tweak a good result months later.

Treat generation as a slow, failing job

  • Anything from a few seconds to a minute. Don’t do it inside a web request. Put it on a job queue and notify the user when it’s done.
  • Timeouts, rate limits, content refusals and the odd empty response. Retry with backoff, but treat a refusal as final rather than retrying the same prompt.
  • Cache results by a hash of the prompt and parameters. Put per-user limits on anything that lets users trigger generation.

Do the exact work in code

Use the model for the creative part only. Background removal (rembg), resizing, palette reduction, cropping, compositing text and packing sprite sheets are all free, fast and deterministic in Python. Most models can’t produce real transparency, so generate on a plain background and remove it. Some of OpenAI’s GPT Image models are an exception with a transparent background option.

If your image needs exact text, like prices or dates, consider generating the artwork without it and adding the text in code. It’s the one way to guarantee it’s spelled right.

Test without spending money

Use a fake provider that returns a fixed image in your unit tests. Keep real API calls for a small set of smoke tests. Use a cheap model for development and switch to the better one in production config.

Integrating with an agent

Image generation and AI agents fit together well. A multimodal agent can write a detailed prompt, call the model, look at the result, critique it and try again. That loop is the part that used to need a human.

Claude doesn’t generate images

If you are using Claude code, you should bear in mind that the built-in model won’t generate raster images like photos or paintings. Anthropic’s help centre says so plainly. Claude can view and analyse images and it can draw diagrams, charts and interactive visuals with code like SVG and HTML.

Its models are aimed at text, code and agents. Claude is very good at the parts around image generation, like writing a detailed prompt and judging whether the result match the brief. You connect it to a specialist image model through a tool and let each do what it’s good at.

  1. The simplest option. If your agent can run shell commands, give it a script like python -m image_gen generate --model meta/muse-image --prompt "..." and tell it where the output goes. That’s what I did.
  2. The Model Context Protocol lets you expose image generation as a tool to any MCP-compatible agent, such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop or Cursor. The agent sees a typed tool with a description rather than having to learn your script.
  3. Function calling in your own agent. If you’re building the agent yourself, define a tool in your LLM API call and run the generation when the model asks for it.

A minimal MCP server in Python looks something like this.

Returning the image itself, not just a file path, lets the agent see what it made.

How the experiments in this guide were run

Every image in this guide was made that way, using Claude Code as the agent with a small Python script for calling the providers. I described what I wanted in plain English. Claude wrote the detailed prompts, picked models from OpenRouter’s price list, ran the script, opened each image and told me honestly what was wrong with it. When OpenRouter changed its API mid-session it found the error, fixed the code and carried on.

Tips for agent-driven generation

  • Let the agent write the prompts. LLMs are very good at turning “a 90s burger poster that doesn’t look AI” into a detailed, structured prompt. The poster prompts in this guide were written that way.
  • Make sure it can see the output. The critique step is where the value is. An agent that can’t view the image is just a slow way of calling an API.
  • Put the cost in the tool description. Agents make better decisions when they know a call costs a cent or 15 cents.
  • A loop that keeps trying to improve an image can run up a bill. Cap the number of calls or the spend per session.
  • Ask the agent to list what’s wrong with each image, not just whether it’s done. It was the agent that spotted the 2010s milkshake cup in my 1996 poster.
  • The agent is good at checking an image against a brief. Deciding whether the brief was right in the first place is still your job.
  • - Generating an image by starting from random noise and removing it step by step, guided by the prompt.
  • - The compressed internal canvas a diffusion model works on. The reason tiny output sizes don’t work.
  • - How many denoising passes a diffusion model makes. More is slower and usually better, up to a point.
  • - A model trained to produce good results in a few steps, like Flux Schnell or SDXL Turbo.
  • - The random starting point. Same seed, prompt and model gives the same image, where supported.
  • - The part of a model that splits text into chunks. The reason older models couldn’t spell.
  • - The unit a multimodal model counts output in. For images, a fixed number per size and quality.
  • - A model you can download and run yourself, like Flux or SDXL.
  • - A small add-on that teaches an open model a new style or subject without retraining it.
  • - A way to make a diffusion model follow a sketch, pose or depth map.
  • - Regenerating only a masked part of an image.
  • - A metadata standard that records how an image was made, including whether AI was involved.
  • - Google’s invisible watermark for AI-generated content.
  • - The Model Context Protocol, a standard way to give AI agents access to tools.
  • - A resize method that copies pixels rather than blending them. Essential for pixel art.
  • - A view with no perspective. Useful prompt language for top-down shots.

The “Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon” is a game where players try to connect any actor to Kevin Bacon in fewer than six steps, where each step links two actors who co-starred in a film.

The conventional wisdom is that Kevin Bacon is the all-encompassing center of Hollywood, so prolific that the game is a lot easier than if it were called the “Six Degrees of John Doe.”

Samuel L. Jackson is the , with a remoteness of just 2.09. Willem Dafoe is second at 2.13, and Robert De Niro follows at 2.14.

Women are underrepresented among the top 100, taking only 16 spots. Nicole Kidman is the highest-ranking woman at #21.

Let’s create a time machine for the center of Hollywood and calculate actors’ remoteness in previous years. Our time machine starts at the end of 2025.

Let’s time travel to 2006, when Samuel L. Jackson took the crown.

Kevin Bacon still does not appear; his highest rank was #108 in 1996 after his role in “Sleepers.”

We can view all centers of Hollywood since 1980. Use the slider to look around.

How might we predict who will take the crown from Samuel L. Jackson? Let’s apply this idea to the .

To do that, we need to find what affects an actor’s remoteness score.

One obvious metric is film count. Indeed, Samuel L. Jackson appeared in far more films than anyone else in our 169,000 actor dataset. Nicolas Cage, who’s the next closest, appeared in 96 films.

While the relationship between film count and remoteness is strong, it doesn't fully explain actors’ scores. For example, Natalie Portman and Anna Kendrick differ significantly in their remoteness, despite appearing in the same number of films.

The difference between Natalie Portman and Anna Kendrick lies in their co-stars: Natalie Portman is cast in films with more prolific actors than Anna Kendrick. Of the 250 most-connected actors, Natalie Portman has worked with almost three times as many as Anna Kendrick has.

So if you work with more “big dog” actors compared to someone with the same film count, you'll almost certainly be closer to the center of Hollywood. Consequently, co-star film count is the next important factor: this is an actor’s 50 most prolific co-stars by number of films, taken as an average.

Test your knowledge with a few examples: for these actors with similar film counts, who do you think works with more “big dogs” and is more connected to all of Hollywood?

We now have everything we need to predict the future Samuel L. Jackson using film count and co-star data. Our contenders are 99 actors born since 1997 (i.e., Gen Z) who have appeared in at least 5 films.

For the prediction, we need to model actors’ film count and co-star trajectory. To do this, we look at what has happened to actors with similar data in the past.

When predicting film count, consider Sydney Sweeney, who has appeared in 16 films since her debut 15 years ago. By the same point in his career, Robert De Niro also racked up 16 films, and he went on to have a brilliant career totalling 87. By contrast, Chevy Chase reached the same 16-film milestone, but ultimately only appeared in 27 total.

Conversely, after 47 years in Hollywood, Kevin Bacon has a similar film count to Helen Mirren and Gene Hackman.

You'll remember Gene Hackman from the time machine; Kevin Bacon could have been the center of Hollywood if he were born 20 years earlier.

To model a Gen Z actor’s trajectory, we consider comparable careers based on film count and career age, randomly selecting one weighted by similarity.

By applying the same approach for co-star film count, we can start predicting.

To achieve a stable result, we'll run the simulation 10,000 times and see who comes out on top.

The most wins across the 10,000 simulations:

    Chloë Grace Moretz is the most likely Samuel L. Jackson for Gen Z, winning over 10% of simulations. It’s by no means a landslide: her median remoteness is 2.19 and median projected film count is 66, quite far from Samuel L. Jackson’s stratospheric numbers of 116 career films and a 2.09 remoteness score.

    As time goes on, Samuel L. Jackson will eventually stop appearing in films and have fewer connections to new actors, lowering his remoteness score.

    Meanwhile, younger actors will continue starring in films and overtake his status as the center of Hollywood. What we don’t know, however, is exactly how long that will take.
